subject: St Gregory of Nazianzus (Gregory the Theologian, Gregory Nazianzen)
sources_folder: C:/Users/Light/Desktop/claude/theology compass/design/saints-hub/sources/people/gregory-of-nazianzus/ (gitignored). Every text quoted below is saved there as .txt; the file names are given in the notes.

text_used.text: Every quotation of Gregory below is checked word for word (case-insensitive, footnote numbers removed, whitespace normalised) against the translation of Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894), from CCEL's plain-text copy of the whole volume, split into one file per oration (npnf207-oration-NN.txt), the letters (npnf207-select-letters.txt) and the editors' introduction (npnf207-prolegomena-*.txt). 'exact' is the translation as printed. 'display' applies the site's capitals rule for every pronoun for God. Chapter links go to CCEL's page for each oration or letter; each was fetched (HTTP 200) and the quoted line found on it.
text_used.source: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow (tr.), Gregory Nazianzen, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7 (1894), CCEL plain text, marked 'Rights: Public Domain'
text_used.note: Section numbers: NPNF prints Arabic numbers in Orations 2, 7, 8, 18, 42 and 43, and Roman numerals in 1 and 27 to 45. In Oration 27 NPNF's numbering runs one ahead of the Greek editions after section 3 (NPNF V holds the 'breath' line). Pages name the work and section in words only. Oration 14 (On Love of the Poor) and Letter 130 are NOT in NPNF; see their items. New Advent (newadvent.org/fathers/3102NN.htm) carries a lightly modernised copy of the same translation (e.g. 'glorify Him' for NPNF's 'glorify ye Him'); quote the NPNF wording.

born.text: Born about 329, at Arianzus, his father's country estate near the small town of Nazianzus in Cappadocia, in central Turkey today. The Catholic Encyclopedia says about 325; Britannica and the Episcopal Church say about 330. The site of Nazianzus is not certain: the 1894 NPNF editors put its ruins about eighteen miles south-east of Aksaray (they write 'Ak Serai'), at the foot of Hasan Dagh; Britannica says the exact location is not known.
born.source: OCA, 'Saint Gregory the Theologian' ('born ... in the year 329, at Arianzos (not far from the city of Cappadocian Nazianzos)'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('born at Arianzus ... c. 325'); Britannica ('born c. 330, Arianzus, near Nazianzus, in Cappadocia ... [now in Turkey]'; 'the exact location of which is not known'); NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('born at Arianzus, a country estate belonging to his father'; 'about eighteen miles south-east of Ak Serai ... Hassan Dagh')
born.note: Collins (via Dictionary.com) says ?329. The NPNF editors argue from his poem on his own life for 'not earlier than 330'. Plain wording that holds: 'Born about 329 (some say 325 or 330)'. Files: cal-oca-gregory-jan25.txt, ref-catholic-encyclopedia-1910-gregory.txt, ref-britannica.txt, npnf207-prolegomena-life.txt.

family.text: His father, also Gregory, had belonged to a small sect (the Hypsistarians), was won to the faith by his wife Nonna, and became bishop of Nazianzus. Nonna promised Gregory to God before he was born. He had an older sister, Gorgonia, and a younger brother, Caesarius, a court physician. All four are honoured as saints.
family.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life; Oration 18, section 11 ('it was on her part a great undertaking to promise me to God before my birth'); OCA life (father 1 January, Nonna 5 August, Caesarius 9 March); The Roman Martyrology (1916): Caesarius 25 February ('whom his brother blessed Gregory the Theologian, says he saw among the hosts of the Blessed'), Nonna 5 August ('St. Nonna, mother of blessed Gregory Nazianzen'), Gorgonia 9 December ('sister of blessed Gregory the Theologian, who has related her virtues and miracles')
family.note: The NPNF editors say Gorgonia was 'probably somewhat older' and Caesarius 'perhaps younger'; say 'an older sister' only with that hedge, or just 'a sister and a brother'. Martyrology day headings are OCR-garbled in the saved copy but readable (Twenty-fifth Day of February; Fifth Day of August; Ninth Day of December). File: cal-roman-martyrology-1916.txt.

grew_up.text: Grew up at Nazianzus and Arianzus. Studied at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Caesarea in Palestine and Alexandria, then about ten years at Athens with Basil, leaving at about thirty.
grew_up.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('The saint's studies at Athens ... extended over some ten years; and when he departed in 356 ... he was about thirty years of age'); NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('He seems to have gone there at about the age of eighteen, and not to have left till he was past thirty'); Oration 7, section 6
grew_up.note: Dates for Athens differ: Britannica c. 351-356; NPNF 'probably did not leave the place till 357'; OCA says he left in 358.

died.text: Died at Arianzus, where he was born, probably in 389 or 390, after years of illness. The Orthodox keep 25 January as the day he died.
died.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('The exact date of his death is unknown, but from a passage in Jerome ... it may be assigned, with tolerable certainty, to the year 389 or 390'; 'continuous illness and severe sufferings ... which assailed him during his last years'); OCA ('He died on January 25, 389'); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117 ('died, three years or more ago, in the reign of Theodosius'); Church of England calendar ('379 and 389'); Episcopal LFF 2022 ('his death in 389')
died.note: The 1894 NPNF editors say 'He died in 391'. Britannica: c. 389. Wikidata's 26 January 389 is not used. No ancient text gives the cause beyond illness and age; no last words are recorded. Files: jerome-illustrious-men.txt, ref-catholic-encyclopedia-1910-gregory.txt.

buried.text: Buried at Nazianzus. In 950 his relics were moved to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople. Part later came to Rome, where Pope Gregory XIII moved them into a chapel of St Peter's. On 27 November 2004 Pope John Paul II gave relics of Gregory and of John Chrysostom back to Patriarch Bartholomew in Constantinople. His head is kept at Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos, says the OCA.
buried.source: OCA life ('Saint Gregory was buried at Nazianzos. In the year 950, his holy relics were transferred to Constantinople into the church of the Holy Apostles. Later on, a portion of his relics was transferred to Rome'); OCA, 'The transfer of the relics of Saint Gregory the Theologian' (19 January: 'His honorable head is reverently kept in Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos'; 'Until the year 1204, when the Western Crusaders captured Constantinople, portions of Saint Gregory's relics were kept in the church of Hagia Sophia, in the church of the Holy Apostles, and in the church of the Holy Resurrection'); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 11 June ('the translation of St. Gregory Nazianzen, whose sacred body after having been brought from Constantinople to Rome ... was, by the Sovereign Pontiff, Gregory XIII., transferred with great solemnity to a chapel of the basilica of St. Peter'); Letter of John Paul II to Bartholomew I, 27 November 2004
buried.note: The year of the St Peter's move (1580 on a Commons painting of the procession) is NOT checked; print 'under Pope Gregory XIII' (pope 1572-1585). That the relics were carried off in 1204 is said in 2004 news reports, not in the Vatican letter; the OCA only says they were in Constantinople 'until the year 1204'. Files: cal-oca-relics-jan19.txt, relics-2004-vatican-letter.txt, cal-roman-martyrology-1916.txt.

also_called.text: Gregory the Theologian, in the Orthodox Church. OCA: 'Saint Gregory the Theologian, Archbishop of Constantinople'. Greek: 'Ὁ Ἅγιος Γρηγόριος ὁ Θεολόγος'. Russian: 'Григорий Богослов', also 'Назианзин'.
also_called.source: OCA life; synaxarion.gr (Great Synaxaristes), 25 January; azbyka.ru
also_called.note: Both the NPNF editors and the Catholic Encyclopedia say he shares the title 'the Theologian' with St John the Evangelist alone. Files: cal-synaxarion-gr-1881.txt, cal-azbyka-grigorij-bogoslov.txt.

also_called.text: Gregory Nazianzen, in the Catholic calendar. USCCB: 'Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, Bishops and Doctors of the Church'.
also_called.source: USCCB readings page for 2 January 2026; The Roman Martyrology (1916), 9 May

also_called.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, in the Church of England, the Episcopal Church and the Lutheran calendars.
also_called.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar; Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; Lutheran Service Book list (CPH)

also_called.text: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, with Basil the Great and John Chrysostom, kept together on 30 January in the East.
also_called.source: OCA, 'Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs'; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910, 'Doctors of the Church'; Britannica

also_called.text: 'The Great': the 1894 NPNF editors say the Council of Ephesus (431) called him this.
also_called.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life, first sentence
also_called.note: Not checked in the acts of Ephesus. Do not print until checked.

status.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans, and remembered by Lutherans. A Doctor of the Church for Catholics, one of the four great Greek doctors. No church has ever questioned him.
status.source: USCCB ('Bishops and Doctors of the Church'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910, 'Doctors of the Church' (in the East 'three Doctors were pre-eminent: St. John Chrysostom, St. Basil, and St. Gregory Nazianzen'; Pius V's Breviary of 1568 raised 'the feasts of the four Greek Doctors' to doubles); OCA; Church of England; Episcopal LFF 2022; LCMS; ELCA
status.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia gives no single date when he was 'declared' a Doctor; say 'a Doctor of the Church', not 'declared in 1568'. File: ref-catholic-encyclopedia-doctors.txt.

patron_of.text: Poets, students, teachers and orthodoxy, says Britannica.
patron_of.source: Britannica: 'He is venerated as a patron saint of poets, students, teachers, and orthodoxy.'
patron_of.note: The only source found. Wikidata's four patronages of places (e.g. Pozoblanco) are not checked and not used.

in_art.text: In Byzantine art: a bishop with a high forehead and a full grey beard, in a white stole marked with black crosses, holding a book of the Gospels. Often shown with Basil and John Chrysostom as the Three Hierarchs.
in_art.source: The Pammakaristos mosaic (Istanbul, about 1310) and the Kyiv St Sophia mosaic already on the site; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910, 'Doctors of the Church' ('The three are as common in Eastern art as the four are in Western. Durandus ... remarks that Doctors should be represented with books in their hands')
in_art.note: The look is my reading of the two mosaics, not a quoted source. A written description of his face exists, by the 19th-century historian Ullmann as quoted in NPNF: 'Gregory was of middle height and somewhat pale; but his pallor became him. His hair was thick and blanched by age, his short beard and conspicuous eyebrows were thicker. On his right eye he had a scar.' The OCA: 'of medium height and somewhat pale. He had thick eyebrows, and a short beard.' Ullmann's ancient source is not given; if printed, say 'a 19th-century historian, drawing on Gregory's own poems' only after a check, or just 'the OCA's life says'. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Split into short sentences on the page.

wrote.text: 45 orations (sermons and speeches), 243 letters and 507 poems survive, by the count of the 1894 NPNF editors. Jerome, his pupil, counted his writings at about thirty thousand lines.
wrote.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Writings ('The Orations.--These--forty-five in number'; 'The Letters, of which two hundred and forty-three are extant'; 'The Poems, five hundred and seven in number'); OCA ('In all, forty-five of Saint Gregory's orations have been preserved'); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117 ('composed works, amounting in all to thirty thousand lines')
wrote.note: Modern editions count letters and poems a little differently: say 'by the count of the 1894 editors'. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'Jerome and Suidas say that Gregory wrote more than 30,000 verses'; Jerome's own words are 'works ... thirty thousand lines', so do not say 'verses' on Jerome's word. He wrote no Bible commentaries (Britannica: 'Though Gregory wrote no commentaries'). File: npnf207-prolegomena-writings.txt.

pronounced.source: Collins English Dictionary, Complete and Unabridged (2012), entry 'Gregory of Nazianzus', read on Dictionary.com; Wiktionary gives the same IPA
pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster has no entry (404). Collins's own site answered 403. The same Collins entry wrongly calls him 'bishop of Caesarea (370-79)', which was Basil (see misquoted). No dictionary respelling found for 'Nazianzen'. Files: ref-dictionary-com-pronunciation.txt, ref-wiktionary-nazianzus.txt.

roles.text: Student: about ten years at Athens, with Basil.
roles.note: Suggested line under the role: 'Ten years at Athens, with Basil'.

roles.text: Priest: ordained by his father against his will, probably at Christmas 361; he ran to Basil in Pontus and came back by Easter 362.
roles.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('ordained his son to the Priesthood, much against the will of the said son ... probably at Christmas of the year 361'; 'present in the Church on Easter day 362'); Oration 1, section 1 ('the noble tyranny which I have suffered'); Oration 2; Episcopal LFF 2022 ('In 361, against his will')
roles.note: Britannica says 362. Suggested line: 'Ordained by force, 361'.

roles.text: Bishop of Sasima, which he never took up: consecrated by Basil about 372 to hold a disputed border town; he stayed at Nazianzus to help his father.
roles.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('to one of these, Sasima, a miserable little village he consecrated his friend Gregory, almost by force'; 'it is probable he never actually administered'); Britannica ('reluctantly accepted consecration (372) to the episcopate for the village of Sasima. He never took possession of the bishopric'); Letters 48 to 50

roles.text: Bishop of Constantinople: led the small Nicene church there from 379, was installed in the great church by the emperor Theodosius in November 380, presided for a time at the Council of 381, and resigned in June 381.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 (proceeded to Constantinople early in 379; in November 380 the emperor accompanied him to St Sophia; 'In June, 381, he preached a farewell sermon'); Britannica; Socrates, Church History, Book 5, chapter 7
roles.note: The OCA dates Theodosius's arrival 24 November 380; Socrates dates the Arians' expulsion 26 November. Suggested line: '379 to 381'.

roles.text: Poet in retirement: back at Arianzus from about 383 until his death, writing most of his poems.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('This was toward the end of the year 383 ... immediately withdrew to Arianzus'; 'During the six years of life which remained to him ... composed, in all probability, the greater part of the copious poetical works')

catholic.text: 2 January, a memorial, shared with St Basil the Great. The 1916 Roman Martyrology kept him on 9 May, and kept 11 June for the move of his relics into St Peter's.
catholic.source: USCCB readings page for 2 January 2026 ('Memorial of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, Bishops and Doctors of the Church'); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 9 May ('At Nazianzus, the birthday of St. Gregory, bishop and doctor of the church, surnamed the Theologian, because of his remarkable knowledge of divinity. At Constantinople, he restored the Catholic faith, which was fast waning, and repressed the rising heresies.') and 11 June; the Martyrology's index: 'Gregory Nazianzen, St., B., the May 9'
catholic.note: The move from 9 May to 2 January came with the 1969 reform of the calendar: I did not fetch a document that states it; the site can simply print both, the 1916 date labelled as the 1916 Martyrology. The current (2004) Martyrology was not checked. Files: cal-usccb-2026-01-02.txt, cal-roman-martyrology-1916.txt.

orthodox.text: 25 January, his own day, in the OCA, the Greek churches and the Russian Church (7 February on today's civil calendar for churches on the old calendar). 30 January, the Three Holy Hierarchs, with Basil and John Chrysostom (12 February on the old calendar). The OCA also keeps 19 January for the transfer of his relics.
orthodox.source: OCA pages: 'Saint Gregory the Theologian' (commemorated January 25), 'Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs' (January 30), 'The transfer of the relics of Saint Gregory the Theologian' (commemorated January 19); synaxarion.gr: 'Ὁ Ἅγιος Γρηγόριος ὁ Θεολόγος Ἀρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως', 25 Ιανουαρίου; azbyka.ru: 'Дни памяти 7 февраля, 12 февраля'
orthodox.note: Unlike Martin, the Eastern date does not differ between churches: 25 January everywhere checked. Why 30 January: the OCA says the three hierarchs appeared to St John of Euchaita in 1084 and ended a quarrel over which of them was greatest; the Catholic Encyclopedia tells the same story from the Menaion and notes that sermons for the feast are older (Cosmas Vestitor, 10th century). GOARCH not checked (blocked for Martin; not tried again). azbyka.ru lists no separate 1 February (19 January old calendar) date for the relics. Files: cal-oca-*.txt, cal-synaxarion-gr-1881.txt, cal-azbyka-grigorij-bogoslov.txt.

old_calendar_note.text: Churches on the old (Julian) calendar keep each date 13 days later on today's calendar: 25 January falls on 7 February, and 30 January on 12 February.

anglican.text: 2 January, with Basil, a Lesser Festival in the Church of England: 'Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus, Bishops, Teachers of the Faith, 379 and 389'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in roman type, not italic, which marks a Lesser Festival rather than a Commemoration)
anglican.note:
Checked in the page's HTML: the entry is a plain

, while the Commemoration below it (Seraphim of Sarov) is in . File: cal-church-of-england.txt.

episcopal.text: 9 May: 'Gregory of Nazianzus, Bishop and Theologian, 389'.
episcopal.source: The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar for May and pp. 223-224
episcopal.note: The Episcopal Church keeps Basil separately (not checked here). File: cal-episcopal-lff-2022.txt.

lutheran_lcms.text: 10 January, with Basil and Gregory of Nyssa: 'Basil the Great of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, Pastors and Confessors'.
lutheran_lcms.source: Concordia Publishing House (the LCMS publisher), 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations', taken from Lutheran Service Book pp. xii-xiii
lutheran_lcms.note: The 2008 Lutheran Witness page used for Martin does not list January. File: cal-cph-commemorations.txt.

lutheran_elca.text: 14 June, with Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina: 'Gregory of Nazianzus, Bishop of Constantinople, c. 389'.
lutheran_elca.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year, final draft January 2006 (archived)
lutheran_elca.note: Same source class as Martin's ELCA date: a 2006 final draft, not the printed book or a current ELCA page. File: cal-elca-elw-draft-2006.txt.

coptic.text: No own day found in the Coptic Synaxarium on copticchurch.net (all 390 day pages scanned for his names). He is only mentioned in other saints' entries (Hator 21, Bashons 7, Paona 2).
coptic.source: copticchurch.net Synaxarium, all day pages scanned 2026-09-24
coptic.note: Leave the Coptic Church off the page. The Bashons 7 entry (on Athanasius) calls him 'Gregory the Theologian, the writer of the liturgy'. A search result claimed Tobi 24; that page (saved as cal-coptic-tobi-24.txt) has no Gregory.

why_they_differ.text: The East keeps 25 January, the day he died. Rome kept 9 May until the 20th-century reform, and since then keeps him with Basil on 2 January, the day after Basil's death (1 January). The Church of England follows Rome's pairing; the Episcopal Church and the ELCA keep other days.
why_they_differ.source: OCA ('He died on January 25, 389'); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 9 May; USCCB; NPNF Oration 43 heading ('S. Basil died January 1, a.d. 379')
why_they_differ.note: Only the facts are sourced; no source I read says WHY 2 January was chosen. Print the dates and the day of death; do not print a reason for 2 January.

numbers.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Writings ('These--forty-five in number'); OCA ('In all, forty-five of Saint Gregory's orations have been preserved')
numbers.note: Chip suggestion: 'Orations' 45; lines 'Sermons and speeches', 'Five won him the name Theologian'.

numbers.note: Chip suggestion: 'Poems' 507; lines 'Most written in retirement', 'Plus 243 letters'.

numbers.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117 ('composed works, amounting in all to thirty thousand lines')
numbers.note: Jerome knew him. Chip suggestion: 'Lines, by Jerome's count' 30,000.

numbers.text: About 10 years at Athens, leaving at about 30.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('some ten years ... he was about thirty years of age'); NPNF prolegomena ('not to have left till he was past thirty')
numbers.note: Chip suggestion: 'Years at Athens' 10; lines 'With Basil', 'Left at about 30'.

numbers.text: 150 bishops at the council of 381, which he chaired for a time before he resigned.
numbers.source: NPNF Oration 42 title ('The Last Farewell in the Presence of the One Hundred and Fifty Bishops'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('One hundred and fifty bishops met in council, in May, 381')

numbers.text: About 7 months as bishop in the great church of Constantinople (November 380 to June 381); about 2 years in the city before that.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('In November, the emperor entered the city'; 'In June, 381, he preached a farewell sermon'; 'which he had held for only a few months'); Gibbon, chapter 27 ('in the space of two years')
numbers.note: '7 months' is my arithmetic from two sourced dates; the source says 'only a few months'. Use 'A few months' in words, or leave this number out.

traits.text: A lover of quiet. When Basil called him lazy for not taking up Sasima, he answered: 'My greatest business always is to keep free from business.'
traits.source: Letter 49, to Basil ('You accuse me of laziness and idleness, because I did not accept your Sasima'); also Oration 2, sections 6 and 7 ('an eager longing for the blessings of calm and retirement')
traits.note: Exact and display are the same. Trait title suggestion: 'busy doing nothing' or 'fond of quiet'.

traits.text: A teasing wit. He mocked Basil's beloved hermitage as 'your mousehole with the stately names of Abode of Thought, Monastery, School', and ended: 'This is perhaps too long for a letter, but it is too short for a comedy.' Jerome says that when he asked him about a hard Bible word, Gregory 'playfully evaded' him with a joke about applause in church.
traits.source: Letter 4, to Basil; Jerome, Letter 52, section 8
traits.note: Jerome's letter: New Advent (NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, tr. W. H. Fremantle, 1893). File: jerome-letter-52.txt.

traits.text: Quick to tears. Preaching at his brother's funeral, he had promised not to grieve too much, then stopped: 'how can I recall those days without my tears showing that, contrary to my promises, my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint?'
traits.source: Oration 7, On his brother Caesarius, sections 1 and 6

traits.text: Hurt easily, but would not take revenge. Years after the Sasima affair he still called it 'a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated'. Yet when Julian's persecution ended he told Christians: 'Let us conquer those that have oppressed us, with clemency'. When a mob stoned his congregation, he wrote that it is 'far greater and more Godlike, to bear with injuries'.
traits.source: Oration 43, section 59 (NPNF); Oration 5, Second Invective against Julian, section 37 (tr. C. W. King, 1888, PD, on tertullian.org); Letter 77, to Theodore (NPNF)
traits.note: Oration 5 is not in NPNF: King's 1888 translation (Gregory Nazianzen, Julian the Emperor) is public domain; file oration-05-king-1888-tertullian-org.txt, URL https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_nazianzen_3_oration5.htm. Letter 77 page: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf207/npnf207.iv.iv.vii.i.html .

others_on_him.text: 'Gregory, bishop of Nazianzen, a most eloquent man, and my instructor in the Scriptures'
others_on_him.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, tr. E. C. Richardson, 1892)
others_on_him.note: Jerome studied with him at Constantinople (Catholic Encyclopedia). Jerome also calls him 'My teacher, Gregory of Nazianzus' (Letter 52, section 8).

others_on_him.text: 'Gregory, who far excelled in eloquence and piety all those of the age in which he lived'
others_on_him.source: Socrates Scholasticus, Church History, Book 5, chapter 7 (about 440; NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, rev. A. C. Zenos, 1890)
others_on_him.note: Socrates also (Book 4, chapter 26) on Basil and Gregory: 'he would find it difficult to decide to which of them he ought to assign the pre-eminence'. Files: socrates-church-history-book4.txt, socrates-church-history-book5.txt. CHECKER 2026-09-25: No source read dates Socrates to "about 440"; Book 5 itself mentions the reign of Theodosius the Younger. The page now says "writing in the next century".

others_on_him.text: 'For, as long before us Gregory Nazianzen of reverend memory has taught, one and the same exhortation does not suit all'
others_on_him.source: St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Book 3, Prologue (about 590; NPNF 2nd series vol. 12, tr. J. Barmby, 1895)
others_on_him.note: Ties him to the Christian Personality Test, which is built on Pastoral Rule Book 3. File: gregory-the-great-pastoral-rule-book3.txt.

others_on_him.text: 'The title of Saint has been added to his name: but the tenderness of his heart, and the elegance of his genius, reflect a more pleasing lustre on the memory of Gregory Nazianzen.'
others_on_him.source: Edward Gibbon, The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 27 (1781; Project Gutenberg #733)
others_on_him.note: A later and sceptical voice, not a contemporary: use only if the section allows one. File: gibbon-decline-and-fall-ch27.txt.

life_moments.text: PLACE: At sea off Cyprus. WHEN: A young man, not yet baptised. TITLE: The storm. He sailed from Alexandria for Athens in November, out of season. A storm hit, the water jars broke, and the ship would not answer the helm. He was not yet baptised, and he was most afraid of dying unbaptised. He prayed and vowed himself to God, and the crew prayed with him. The sea calmed, and they reached Rhodes. He kept his vow.
life_moments.source: Oration 18, On his father, section 31 ('While we were all in fear of a common death, spiritual death was what I was most afraid of; for I was in danger of departing in misery, being unbaptised'; 'we promised ourselves if we were saved, to God, and, when we had been saved, gave ourselves to Him'); NPNF prolegomena, The Life (November; the water tanks; off Cyprus)
life_moments.note: The OCA adds that the storm lasted twenty days; not in Oration 18 (it may come from his poem on his life, not checked). The wonders in this story are in the miracles section.

life_moments.text: PLACE: Athens. WHEN: About ten years, from his late teens. TITLE: One soul in two bodies. He met Basil again and they became inseparable. They knew only two roads, one to church and one to their teachers. 'We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.' Among the students was the future emperor Julian, and Gregory says he saw trouble in him even then.
life_moments.source: Oration 43, On Basil, sections 20 and 21; Oration 5, section 24 (King: 'What an evil the Roman world is breeding!')
life_moments.note: 'Two ways were known to us ... the one leading to our sacred buildings and the teachers there, the other to secular instructors' (43.21).

life_moments.text: PLACE: Nazianzus. WHEN: Christmas 361 to Easter 362. TITLE: Ordained by force. His aged father and the people made him a priest against his will. He ran off to Basil in Pontus. He came back by Easter and preached his first sermon, forgiving 'the noble tyranny which I have suffered'. Then he wrote a long defence of why he ran: guiding people, he said, is 'the art of arts and science of sciences'.
life_moments.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life; Oration 1, section 1; Oration 2, section 16
life_moments.note: Oration 2 was probably never preached aloud (NPNF introduction to Oration 2). It became a source for John Chrysostom's On the Priesthood and Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule (NPNF prolegomena; Catholic Encyclopedia).

life_moments.text: PLACE: Sasima. WHEN: About 372. TITLE: A bishop against his will. Basil, now archbishop and fighting a rival bishop over a newly split province, made Gregory bishop of Sasima, a poor village on the border, to hold it. Gregory refused to go. He wrote to Basil: 'Give me before all things quiet. Why should I fight for sucking pigs and fowls, and those not my own, as though for souls and canons?' The friendship never fully healed.
life_moments.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life; Letters 48 to 50; Oration 43, section 59; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('an estrangement between Basil and himself which was never altogether removed')

life_moments.text: PLACE: Constantinople. WHEN: 379 to 380. TITLE: The Anastasia. The city's churches were held by the Arians. Gregory came to the small Nicene flock and preached in a relative's house, which he called Anastasia, 'Resurrection'. There he gave the five Theological Orations. At the Easter vigil a mob burst in and threw stones, and a man was killed. He asked his people not to seek revenge.
life_moments.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life (Anastasia; 'hiring an assassin'); Oration 42, sections 26 and 27 ('Farewell my Anastasia'; 'Remember my stonings'); Letter 77, to Theodore; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('actually attacked in his own chapel, whilst baptizing his Easter neophytes'); Gibbon, chapter 27 ('as a man lost his life in the affray'); OCA ('killing one bishop and wounding Saint Gregory', and the date 21 April 379)
life_moments.note: Who died differs: Gibbon says 'a man', the OCA says 'one bishop'. Print 'someone was killed' or leave it out. The OCA and NPNF also tell of an assassin sent to kill him who came to him in tears instead (from his poem on his life; no public-domain English checked).

life_moments.text: PLACE: Constantinople. WHEN: May to June 381. TITLE: The farewell. The emperor Theodosius put him in the great church. At the council of 381 he became president, but his peace plan for Antioch was shouted down, and late-arriving bishops said his move from Sasima broke the church's rules. He resigned in a great farewell speech: 'give me my desert, my country life, and my God'.
life_moments.source: Oration 42, sections 24 to 27; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 (the council; 'a cry like that of a flock of jackdaws'); Socrates, Church History, Book 5, chapter 7; Gibbon, chapter 27
life_moments.note: Socrates says he resigned 'understanding that some murmured at his preferment because he was a stranger'. The 'jackdaws' line is from his poem on his life, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (translator not named); do not print it as his words without a PD translation.

life_moments.text: PLACE: Arianzus. WHEN: About 383 until his death. TITLE: Home to the garden. He handed Nazianzus to his cousin Eulalius and went home. He wrote poems by a spring and a shady walk, wrote letters against the teaching of Apollinarius, and in 382 kept a whole Lent in silence.
life_moments.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('his cousin Eulalius'; 'by a fountain near which there was a shady walk, his favourite resort'); NPNF prolegomena ('his sole luxuries were a garden and a fountain'); Britannica ('even during one year when he took a vow of silence for Lent'); Letters 101 and 102 to Cledonius
life_moments.note: The Lent of silence: Britannica gives no year; 382 is in the fathers research (not checked). Print 'he once kept a whole Lent in silence'.

summary.text: The early sources record wonders in Gregory's own life and family, and he tells them himself, in his funeral speeches. He works no wonders of his own in them. They are: the storm at sea; a light at his father's baptism; his father healed at Easter; his mother healed after a dream of him; his sister Gorgonia healed at the altar.
summary.source: Oration 18, sections 12, 13 and 28 to 31; Oration 8, sections 16 to 18
summary.note: Frame the section as 'Wonders he told'. He expected disbelief and said so (see 'expected_doubt').

items.text: TITLE: The storm. PLACE: At sea, bound for Greece. WHO SAW IT: Gregory, the crew, and a boy on board. STORY: As the storm raged, his parents at home learned of his danger in a dream and prayed. Gregory dreamed of a Fury. A boy on board, fond of him, 'thought he saw my mother walk upon the sea, and seize and drag the ship to land with no great exertion.' The sea began to calm, and they reached Rhodes.
items.note: Exact quote: 'thought he saw my mother walk upon the sea, and seize and drag the ship to land with no great exertion.' Also: 'We had confidence in the vision, for the sea began to grow calm'.

items.text: TITLE: Light at the font. PLACE: Nazianzus, about 325. WHO SAW IT: some of those present, and the bishop baptising him. STORY: As his father came up from the water at his baptism, 'there flashed around him a light and a glory'. Some saw it and kept quiet, each thinking only he had seen it. The bishop who baptised him cried out that he was anointing his own successor.
items.note: Exact: 'there flashed around him a light and a glory worthy of the disposition with which he approached the gift of faith'. The year 325 comes from Britannica (bishops on their way to Nicaea); Gregory says only that bishops were hastening to Nicaea (18.12).

items.text: TITLE: His father at Easter. PLACE: Nazianzus. WHO SAW IT: the whole congregation. STORY: His old father lay dying of fever, his mouth so ulcered he could not swallow water. On Easter night the people prayed in church. At the hour of the mysteries he stirred, called a servant, stood, and said the prayers of the liturgy from his bed. He recovered and led the service the next Sunday.
items.note: Gregory: 'A shudder comes over me as I proceed with my story. And though you, my hearers, may shudder, do not disbelieve'. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Oration 18.29: he "celebrates the mysteries, in such few words as his strength allowed" in "the sanctuary without a sanctuary", at home, not in church. The page no longer says he "prayed the liturgy right there".

items.text: TITLE: Loaves in a dream. PLACE: Nazianzus. WHO SAW IT: his mother, her maids, and Gregory. STORY: His mother could not eat and was near death. She dreamed that Gregory came at night with a basket of white loaves, blessed them, and fed her. In the morning she was better. She told him: 'My child, you most readily and kindly fed me, and then you ask how I am. I am very well and at ease.'
items.note: Exact quote contains two spaces in NPNF after 'am.'; normalised.

items.text: TITLE: Gorgonia at the altar. PLACE: Nazianzus. WHO SAW IT: Gorgonia kept it secret; Gregory and the bishop were told. STORY: His sister was near death from a fever the doctors could not treat. At night she went to the altar, laid her head on it, and would not let go until she was healed. She rubbed the consecrated bread she had kept on her body, mixed with her tears. 'She went away feeling at once that she was saved.'
items.source: Oration 8, On his sister Gorgonia, sections 17 and 18
items.note: Exact: 'and, O the wonder, she went away feeling at once that she was saved'. NPNF's word is 'antitypes of the Precious Body and Blood'. The 1916 Martyrology (9 December) says Gregory 'has related her virtues and miracles'. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Oration 8.17 describes "an extraordinary and malignant disease" with the frame "incessantly fevered"; the page now says a dangerous illness with a constant fever, and cites sections 17 and 18.

expected_doubt.text: He knew he would be doubted, and answered it himself: 'Great though these things be, they are not untrue.' And of his father: 'do not disbelieve'. Of the light at the font: 'to profane minds nothing that is good is trustworthy.'
expected_doubt.note: No early doubter by name was found. Gibbon (1781), on the later Anastasia church: 'the credulity of the succeeding age was prepared to believe the miracles and visions' (about miracles attributed to the church later, not about Gregory's own accounts).

later_story.text: A later story: in 1084 the Three Hierarchs appeared in a vision to John, bishop of Euchaita, said they were equal before God, and asked for one shared feast on 30 January.
later_story.source: OCA, Synaxis of the Three Hierarchs; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910, 'Doctors of the Church' (from the Menaion, under Alexius Comnenus)
later_story.note: OCA quotes them: 'There are no divisions among us, and no opposition to one another.' Mark as a later story (seven centuries after Gregory).

framing.text: Gregory wrote a great deal that survives. All lines below are from the 1894 NPNF translation by C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow unless marked.

feature.exact: Farewell, O Trinity, my meditation, and my glory.
feature.display: Farewell, O Trinity, my meditation, and my glory.
feature.greek: Χαῖρέ μοι, ὦ Τριὰς, τὸ ἐμὸν μελέτημα καὶ καλλώπισμα
feature.ctx: The last farewell of his resignation speech, after he had said goodbye to his church, the city, East and West, and the angels.
feature.greek_source: Greek Wikisource, 'Συντακτήριος, εις την των ρν επισκόπων παρουσίαν', section 27 (Migne text); file greek-oration-42-wikisource.txt
feature.note: 'καλλώπισμα' is literally 'adornment, pride'; NPNF renders 'glory'. Alternative feature for a Still Water reader: 'My greatest business always is to keep free from business.' (Letter 49); no Greek found for it.

lines.exact: My greatest business always is to keep free from business.
lines.display: My greatest business always is to keep free from business.
lines.ctx: To Basil, who had called him lazy for not taking up Sasima.

lines.exact: We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.
lines.display: We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.
lines.ctx: On his student years with Basil at Athens.

lines.exact: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
lines.display: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
lines.ctx: Against the teaching that Christ had no human mind.
lines.note: His most quoted line in theology. Often shortened to 'the unassumed is the unhealed' (see misquoted).

lines.exact: Christ is born, glorify ye Him.  Christ from heaven, go ye out to meet Him.  Christ on earth; be ye exalted.
lines.display: Christ is born, glorify ye Him. Christ from heaven, go ye out to meet Him. Christ on earth; be ye exalted.
lines.ctx: The opening of his Christmas sermon. The Orthodox Christmas greeting and the Christmas canon of St Cosmas begin with these words.
lines.work: Oration 38, On the Theophany, or Birthday of Christ
lines.note: Cosmas borrowing: Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh ('later incorporated into the Canon of the Nativity by St. Cosmas of Maiuma'; 'We can also trace the origin of our traditional Christmas greeting ... to this source'), https://archpitt.org/the-traditional-byzantine-celebratlon-of-the-feast-of-the-nativity-of-our-lord/ , file ref-cosmas-archpitt.txt.

lines.exact: Let us become like Christ, since Christ became like us.
lines.display: Let us become like Christ, since Christ became like us.
lines.ctx: From his first sermon as a priest, on Easter day 362.
lines.work: Oration 1, On Easter and his reluctance

lines.exact: No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One.
lines.display: No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One.
lines.ctx: On the Trinity, to people about to be baptised.

lines.exact: For we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath
lines.display: For we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath
lines.ctx: In the first Theological Oration, while warning that not everyone should argue about God at every time.
lines.place: section 5 in NPNF (4 in the Greek editions)
lines.note: The sentence continues: '; and if the expression is permissible, we ought to do nothing else.' The Greek-edition number (4) is from general knowledge, not checked: print no section number.

lines.exact: If a stranger fall at your feet, homeless and a foreigner, welcome in him Him who for your sake was a stranger
lines.display: If a stranger fall at your feet, homeless and a foreigner, welcome in him Him Who for your sake was a stranger
lines.ctx: To the newly baptised, on how to live.

lines.exact: For the guiding of man, the most variable and manifold of creatures, seems to me in very deed to be the art of arts and science of sciences.
lines.display: For the guiding of man, the most variable and manifold of creatures, seems to me in very deed to be the art of arts and science of sciences.
lines.ctx: Why he ran from being made a priest.
lines.work: Oration 2, In Defence of his Flight to Pontus
lines.note: NPNF's footnote: 'This is the original of the frequently quoted commonplace' in Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care, part 1, chapter 1.

more_if_needed.exact: Give me before all things quiet.
I am weary of being charged with my gentleness.
give me my desert, my country life, and my God, Whom alone I may have to please, and shall please by my simple life.
For they seek not for priests, but for orators, not for stewards of souls, but for treasurers of money, not for pure offerers of the sacrifice, but for powerful patrons.
I do not accept this legislation; I do not approve this custom. They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women

This is perhaps too long for a letter, but it is too short for a comedy.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: 'The unassumed is the unhealed.' TRUTH: A modern shortening. His words are: 'For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.'
misquoted_or_legend.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: Not a modern shortening: it is a shorter translation of the first half of his own line. The page now says so ("Close to his words, but only half of them").

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: 'Remember God more often than you breathe.' TRUTH: A loose paraphrase. He wrote: 'we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath; and if the expression is permissible, we ought to do nothing else.' And he says it while warning that not everyone should debate about God at every time.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Oration 27, the First Theological Oration (NPNF section V)

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: 'As a fish cannot swim without water, and a bird cannot fly without air, so a Christian cannot advance a single step without Christ.' TRUTH: Widely shared as his, and printed in the 1894 NPNF introduction, which takes it from a Victorian writer, 'Mr. Crake', with no work of Gregory's named. It is not in any of his orations or letters in NPNF.
misquoted_or_legend.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('In his seclusion, says Mr. Crake, ... "As a fish cannot swim without water, and a bird cannot fly without air, he said, so a Christian cannot advance a single step without Christ."'); searched all NPNF Gregory texts saved locally
misquoted_or_legend.note: Not proven false: it may paraphrase a poem not in NPNF. Word it as 'No work of his is known to contain it'. Quote Investigator has no entry (not found). CHECKER 2026-09-25: The NPNF editors name him only as "Mr. Crake"; nothing read gives his century, so the page no longer says "19th-century". The line occurs once in the whole NPNF 2.7 volume, in the editors' life (checked in the full CCEL text).

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He was bishop of Caesarea. TRUTH: That was Basil. Gregory was made bishop of Sasima (where he never served), helped his father at Nazianzus, and was bishop of Constantinople in 380 and 381. The Collins dictionary entry makes this mistake: 'bishop of Caesarea (370-79)'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Collins English Dictionary via Dictionary.com; NPNF prolegomena; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He and Gregory of Nyssa were brothers. TRUTH: Gregory of Nyssa was Basil's younger brother. Gregory of Nazianzus was their friend. Socrates warned even in the 5th century that 'from the likeness of the name' people confused the Gregorys.
misquoted_or_legend.source: NPNF, Select Letters, introduction to the letters to Gregory of Nyssa ('Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, was a younger brother of Basil the Great'); Socrates, Church History, Book 4, chapter 27 (on Gregory the Wonderworker)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Socrates's warning is about Gregory the Wonderworker, not Nyssa; quote it only as 'people have confused the Gregorys since the 5th century'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He wrote 'Christ Suffering' (Christus Patiens), the first Christian play. TRUTH: It was printed among his works, but its genuineness was doubted by his own Benedictine editors, who put it in an appendix.
misquoted_or_legend.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Writings ('The Benedictine Editors however doubt the genuineness of this Tragedy ... relegates it to an Appendix')

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: The 'Hymn to God' ('O Thou beyond all things') is his. TRUTH: It is printed among his poems, but modern scholars doubt it. A 2018 study calls it an anonymous hymn 'attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus by some authors, but ... most probably composed by a Christian Neoplatonist such as Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Andrei Timotin, 'A Hymn to God Assigned to Gregory of Nazianzus and Its Neoplatonic Context', International Journal of the Platonic Tradition 12.1 (2018), 39-50, abstract via Crossref
misquoted_or_legend.note: Only the abstract was read (Crossref API); the paper itself (Brill; ResearchGate 403) was not. File: ref-timotin-2018-hymn-to-god.txt.

where_he_stood.text: Ten of the quiz's 23 statements. Eight show a line, two are scored but hidden (tears, miracles). All from his own works. Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.nazianzen.cells). Every shown line was found word for word in NPNF (the surplus line is our translation of the Greek) and on the linked page.
where_he_stood.source: which-early-christian.json; NPNF 2nd series vol. 7; Greek text of Oration 14

rows.statement: A good hearty laugh is good for the soul.
rows.line: Who was more kindly in his stories, more refined in his wit, more tender in his rebukes?
rows.work: Funeral Oration on Basil the Great (Oration 43)
rows.note: He is praising Basil's humour, not stating a rule about laughter; the page should say 'of Basil'.

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.line: I take it as admitted by men of sense, that the first of our advantages is education.
rows.work: Funeral Oration on Basil the Great (Oration 43)
rows.note: Cut with a full stop; NPNF continues with a semicolon and goes on to defend 'that external culture which many Christians ill-judgingly abhor'.

rows.statement: If you had to choose, you'd grow closer to God alone in quiet than among other people.
rows.line: For nothing seemed to me so desirable as to close the doors of my senses, and, escaping from the flesh and the world, collected within myself, having no further connection than was absolutely necessary with human affairs, and speaking to myself and to God.
rows.work: In Defence of His Flight to Pontus (Oration 2)
rows.note: NPNF continues with a comma and a footnote mark ('to God, [2561] to live superior to visible things').

rows.statement: Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost.
rows.line: Hidden. The record: Oration 7, sections 1 and 6.
rows.work: Funeral Oration on His Brother Caesarius (Oration 7)
rows.note: If ever shown: 'how can I recall those days without my tears showing that, contrary to my promises, my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint?' (7.6).

rows.statement: Giving to the poor isn't generosity. It's paying back what's already theirs.
rows.line: But look, I beg you, to the first equality, not the later division; not to the law of the one who won the upper hand, but to the law of the One who made us.
rows.note: OUR TRANSLATION from the Greek (Migne text): 'Ἀλλὰ σὺ βλέπε μοι τὴν πρώτην ἰσονομίαν, μὴ τὴν τελευταίαν διαίρεσιν· μὴ τὸν τοῦ κρατήσαντος νόμον, ἀλλὰ τὸν τοῦ κτίσαντος.' Found word for word in section 26 at the URL (file greek-oration-14-blogspot.txt). Oration 14 is not in NPNF. The only free host found is a personal Greek blog; a better free Greek host (Migne scan) would be preferable. The page prints 'the One Who made us' (capital).

rows.statement: God still speaks to people through dreams.
rows.line: For the salvation of my father there was a concurrence of the gradual conviction of his reason, and the vision of dreams which God often bestows upon a soul worthy of salvation.
rows.note: NPNF has a footnote mark after 'conviction'.

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.line: Hidden. The record: Oration 18, sections 13 and 28 to 31; Oration 8, sections 17 and 18.
rows.note: The miracles section of the page carries this material.

rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.line: Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God.
rows.note: NPNF continues '; not to every one; the Subject is not so cheap and low'.

rows.statement: If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to.
rows.line: Now, I had specially pledged myself to become the stay of their old age and the support of their weakness.
rows.work: In Defence of His Flight to Pontus (Oration 2)
rows.note: NPNF continues with a comma: 'a pledge which, to the best of my power, I have fulfilled, even at the expense of philosophy itself'. 'Their' = his parents.

rows.statement: Becoming a better person is mostly down to your own effort.
rows.line: For it is necessary both that we should be our own masters and also that our salvation should be of God.

people.text: Basil the Great: his closest friend from their school days; later the archbishop who made him bishop of Sasima against his will, which hurt the friendship for good.
people.source: Oration 43, sections 20 and 59; Letters 48 to 50; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910

people.text: Gregory the Elder: his father, bishop of Nazianzus, who ordained him priest by force and whom he served as helper until his death in 374.
Nonna: his mother, who won his father to the faith and promised Gregory to God before he was born.
Gorgonia and Caesarius: his sister and brother. He preached both their funerals, and told of Gorgonia's healing at the altar.
Gregory of Nyssa: Basil's younger brother. Gregory scolded him for leaving the Church's service to teach rhetoric, and wrote to him when Basil died.
people.source: NPNF Select Letters, section 2, introduction and Letter 76 ('This, then, was also reserved for my sad life, to hear of the death of Basil')
people.note: Jerome says Nyssa once read a work against Eunomius 'to Gregory Nazianzan and myself' (Lives, chapter 128).

people.text: Jerome: studied the Scriptures with him at Constantinople and called him 'my teacher'.
people.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117; Letter 52, section 8

people.text: Julian the Apostate: a fellow student at Athens, later the emperor who tried to restore paganism. Gregory attacked him in two invectives after his death, yet told Christians not to take revenge on his followers.
people.source: Oration 5, sections 23, 24 and 37 (King, 1888); NPNF prolegomena, The Writings ('The Two Invectives against Julian')

people.text: Maximus the Cynic: a charming adventurer whom Gregory trusted and praised in public, who then had himself secretly consecrated bishop of Constantinople in Gregory's place.
people.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910; Jerome, Lives, chapter 117 (Gregory wrote one work praising Maximus and another 'upbraiding this same Maximus')
people.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: No source says "charming": the NPNF editors and the Catholic Encyclopedia say "a plausible adventurer" who won his confidence. The page now says Gregory "was taken in by an adventurer named Maximus".

people.text: Anthimus of Tyana: the rival bishop whose claim to half of Cappadocia started the Sasima affair; his troops held Sasima, and he taunted Gregory with 'Basilism'.
people.note: Exact: 'reproaching me with Basilism, as if it were a kind of Philipism'.

people.text: Apollinarius of Laodicea: taught that Christ had no human mind. Gregory answered: 'that which He has not assumed He has not healed'.
people.source: Letter 101, to Cledonius; NPNF prolegomena, The Life

people.text: Nectarius: a senator, not yet baptised, chosen bishop of Constantinople after Gregory resigned. Gregory wrote to him kindly afterwards.
people.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('Nectarius, Prefect of the City, who was only a catechumen'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('His two extant letters addressed to Nectarius ... goodwill'); Gibbon, chapter 27
people.note: NPNF calls him Prefect; Gibbon 'the senator Nectarius'. Say 'a leading official'.

how_he_died.text: He spent his last years at Arianzus, the family estate where he was born, ill for much of the time, writing poems and letters. He died there, probably in 389 or 390; the Orthodox keep 25 January. No account of his death, and no last words, survive. His will, which the NPNF editors call probably genuine, left his property to a deacon named Gregory for life, and then to the poor of Nazianzus. His farewell to his church in 381 ended: 'My children, keep, I pray you, that which is committed to your trust. Remember my stonings.'
how_he_died.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910; OCA; Jerome, Lives, chapter 117; NPNF prolegomena, The Life ('he bequeathed all his property to the Deacon Gregory for life, with reversion to the poor of Nazianzus') and The Writings ('his Will, which is probably genuine'); Oration 42, section 27
how_he_died.note: The NPNF editors (quoting 'Mr. Crake', 19th century) add: bed of straw, sackcloth, one tunic, knees worn with kneeling. No ancient source given: if printed, mark as 'a Victorian writer says'. The NPNF editors date the will 'Before leaving Constantinople'. Later history of the relics: see quick_facts.buried (a later story, not his death).

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes, everywhere. Catholics: a saint and Doctor of the Church, memorial 2 January with Basil. Orthodox: 'the Theologian', one of the Three Holy Hierarchs, 25 and 30 January. Church of England: a Lesser Festival, 2 January. Episcopal Church: 9 May. Lutherans: LCMS 10 January, ELCA 14 June. He was never condemned. The OCA says his contemporaries already called him a saint.
is_he_a_saint.source: USCCB; OCA ('His contemporaries already called the archpastor a saint'); Church of England; Episcopal LFF 2022; CPH (LCMS); ELW draft (ELCA); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 9 May ('the birthday of St. Gregory, bishop and doctor of the church, surnamed the Theologian')
is_he_a_saint.note: No 'Blessed', no dropped status, no local-only cult. The only caution is the ELCA source (a 2006 draft), as for Martin.

prayer_he_wrote.exact: O Lord and Maker of all things, and specially of this our frame!  O God and Father and Pilot of men who are Thine!  O Lord of life and death!  O Judge and Benefactor of our souls!  O Maker and Transformer in due time of all things by Thy designing Word, according to the knowledge of the depth of Thy wisdom and providence! do Thou now receive Cæsarius, the firstfruits of our pilgrimage; and if he who was last is first, we bow before Thy Word, by which the universe is ruled; yet do Thou receive us also afterwards, in a time when Thou mayest be found, having ordered us in the flesh as long as is for our profit; yea, receive us, prepared and not troubled by Thy fear, not departing from Thee in our last day, nor violently borne away from things here, like souls fond of the world and the flesh, but filled with eagerness for that blessed and enduring life which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord, to whom be glory, world without end.  Amen.
prayer_he_wrote.display_note: Capitalise 'Whom' in 'to Whom be glory' (Christ). 'Thy', 'Thou', 'Thee', 'Thine' are already capitalised. 'Word' (the Logos) is capitalised in NPNF.
prayer_he_wrote.ctx: The prayer that ends his funeral speech for his younger brother.
prayer_he_wrote.note: Checked word for word (footnote marks removed). A shorter cut for the page: from 'O Lord and Maker of all things' to 'receive us, prepared and not troubled by Thy fear'. This is a prayer TO God that he wrote, which the rules allow.

what_to_read_first.text: Funeral Oration on Basil the Great (Oration 43): his best friend's life, their student days at Athens, and the Sasima hurt, told by Gregory himself.
what_to_read_first.note: HTTP 200, text checked ('We seemed to have one soul').

hard_topics.text: The Sasima quarrel. Basil's side, in Gregory's own report: Basil accused him 'of laziness and idleness'. Gregory's side: 'I throw the blame on your throne, as having on a sudden lifted you above yourself', and, after Basil's death, 'a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated'. The Catholic Encyclopedia: an estrangement 'never altogether removed'.
hard_topics.source: Letters 48 and 49; Oration 43, section 59; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910

hard_topics.text: The invectives against Julian. His own editors call them 'a very dark picture of his character'. Gibbon, a critic: Julian 'has been overwhelmed with a torrent of pious invectives, of which the signal was given by the sonorous trumpet of Gregory Nazianzen'. In the same speech Gregory tells Christians: 'let us not think of confiscation; let us not, bring them before the tribunals; let us not banish them from their country; let us not torture them with scourges'.
hard_topics.source: NPNF prolegomena, The Writings; Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 23 (Gutenberg #732); Oration 5, section 37 (King, 1888)
hard_topics.note: Gibbon quote checked in gibbon-decline-and-fall-ch27.txt (the chapter 23 excerpt is appended there); the footnote number '2' after 'trumpet' is dropped. King's text has a stray comma in 'let us not, bring them'; quote as printed or cut before it. CHECKER 2026-09-25: "a very dark picture of his character" means JULIAN's character (NPNF prolegomena, The Writings). The page now prints "a very dark picture" of Julian, so it does not read as a verdict on Gregory.

hard_topics.text: Remarriage. He held one marriage as the law and was hard on a third: 'The first is law, the second is indulgence, the third is transgression, and anything beyond this is swinish'. In the same sermon he attacked laws that punished wives but not husbands: 'They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women'.

Hell and mercy. He taught an 'unquenchable fire ... eternal for the wicked', adding 'though some may prefer even in this place to take a more merciful view of this fire, worthily of Him That chastises'. His translators' footnote: that view 'is not S. Gregory's own view of the meaning of the passage, though he admits it to be tenable'. Elsewhere he says of those who refuse mercy to penitents: 'Perhaps in it they will be baptized with Fire, in that last Baptism which is more painful and longer'. Readers still argue how hopeful he was.
hard_topics.source: Oration 40, section 36 and footnote 4145; Oration 39, section 19
hard_topics.note: Keep this even-handed: both lines are his; the NPNF footnote is the editors' reading. CHECKER 2026-09-25: "Readers still argue how hopeful he was" had no source read; cut from the page.

hard_topics.text: Ambition and resignation. Critics then said his move to Constantinople broke the church's rule against bishops changing sees; he resigned rather than fight. Gibbon: 'The pride, or the humility, of Gregory prompted him to decline a contest which might have been imputed to ambition and avarice'. He himself asked in his farewell: 'I am weary of being charged with my gentleness.'
hard_topics.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910; Gibbon, chapter 27; Oration 42, section 20
